

## MADM Files {#madm-files}

To use the calculator, you need to create / edit a mad model of the drone (.madm file). This file is split in 2 sections. As a loose analogy to CAD the first is basically like an assembly, and the second section is the parts. You can add comments by using a “\#” like in python.

Here is the .madm file for the subscale as an example, a more detailed explanation of what different lines do is underneath.

rodlineardensity=0.3  
END VARIABLES

scale:0.5 \# drawing scale

add:fuselage,fuselage  
add:battery,battery  
add:wing,wingL  
add:wing,wingR  
add:wingspar,frontwingspar  
add:wingspar,backwingspar  
add:rotorspar,rotorsparL  
add:rotorspar,rotorsparR\# test comment  
add:tailboom,tailboom  
add:tail,tail  
add:tiltservo,tiltL  
add:tiltservo,tiltR  
add:motor,backmotor  \# another test comment  
add:motor,motorL  
add:motor,motorR

modify:motorL,pitchControl,1  
modify:motorR,pitchControl,1  
modify:motorL,rollControl,1  
modify:motorR,rollControl,-1  
modify:backmotor,pitchControl,-1

attach:battery.origin,fuselage.battery  
attach:wingL.rightedge,fuselage.leftspar  
attach:wingR.leftedge,fuselage.rightspar  
attach:frontwingspar.center,fuselage.frontspar  
attach:backwingspar.center,fuselage.backspar  
attach:rotorsparL.farend,wingL.leftrotor  
attach:rotorsparR.farend,wingR.rightrotor  
attach:tailboom.origin,fuselage.origin  
attach:tail.origin,tailboom.farend  
attach:backmotor.origin,tailboom.backmotor  
attach:tiltL.spar,rotorsparL.origin  
attach:tiltR.spar,rotorsparR.origin  
attach:motorL.origin,tiltL.motor  
attach:motorR.origin,tiltR.motor

NEW PART  
name:fuselage  
drawrect:0,-78,150,78  
mass:100  
cg:75,0  
mate:battery,-40,0  
mate:leftspar,130,-78  
mate:rightspar,130,78  
mate:frontspar,130,0  
mate:backspar,200,0

NEW PART  
name:battery  
color:blue  
drawrect:0,-25,100,25  
mass:800  
cg:50,0

NEW PART  
name:wing  
mass:600  
mate:leftedge,60,0  
mate:rightedge,60,720  
mate:leftrotor,136,484  
mate:rightrotor,136,236  
airfoil:270,720,0.25,0,0,wing,xf-ls417-il-100000.csv  
cg:135,360

NEW PART  
specialtype:rod  
name:wingspar  
dx:0  
dy:1200  
lengthdensity:rodlineardensity

NEW PART  
specialtype:rod  
name:rotorspar  
dx:288  
dy:0  
lengthdensity:rodlineardensity

NEW PART  
specialtype:rod  
name:tailboom  
dx:900  
dy:0  
lengthdensity:rodlineardensity  
mate:backmotor,550,0

NEW PART  
name:tail  
mass:150  
cg:-130,0  
airfoil:150,255,0.25,-150,-127.5,stabilizer,xf-naca1408-il-50000.csv  
airfoil:120,130,0.25,-120,-257.5,stabilizer,xf-naca1408-il-50000.csv  
airfoil:120,130,0.25,-120,127.5,stabilizer,xf-naca1408-il-50000.csv

NEW PART  
name:motor  
mass:250  
cg:0,0  
maxthrust:25  
thrustcenter:0,0

NEW PART  
name:tiltservo  
mass:250  
cg:30,0  
drawrect:0,-25,60,25  
mate:spar,60,0  
mate:motor,10,0

Variables allow you to easily modify a property that is common to multiple parts (like in this case the rod linear density, since it was the same for all the carbon fiber spars). Variables must all be defined before the “END VARIABLES” mark. Then just use the variable name anywhere you would have put the number. These are implemented by basically doing “find and replace”, so don’t use variable names with that could appear as part of the file syntax (like “mass”) or make any variable name that is included inside another variable name (like “mass1” and “mass11”).

Parts are defined by a “NEW PART” line. Anything after that line until the next “NEW PART” is interpreted as being properties of that part. These properties are defined by a line which contains the type of property (“name”, “mass”, “cg” …) followed by “:” followed by any parameters split by “,”. Pay attention to the units used, otherwise the results will be completely wrong.  
Coordinate systems for parts are independent and only relative to a reference point in that part. You can use anything as the reference, as long as everything in that part (mates, cg …) are consistent. The X component should indicate forward/backward, with backwards being the positive direction. The Y component should be right/left, with right being the positive direction.

### Generic Part Properties {#generic-part-properties}

**name** \- defines the name for the part so that it can be referenced in the assembly. Names for all parts must be unique

**mass** \- the mass of the part in grams.

**cg** \- the center of gravity. Takes the x and y coordinates in mm (see note on coordinate spaces above)

**maxThrust** \- if the part is a motor, the maximum thrust it can provide in hover, in Newtons. Don’t include this if the part isn’t a motor

**thrustCenter** \- the coordinates (in mm) from which the thrust force acts in hover. Don’t include this if the part isn’t a motor

**drawrect** \- this has no effect on calculations, but draws a rectangle on the diagram to represent the part. Needs coordinates of 2 opposite corners in mm (drawrect:x1,y1,x2,y2)

**color** \- changes the color of the part in the diagram (for drawRect and cg)

**airfoil** \- defines an aerodynamic surface, the parameters are described below

1. Chord length in mm  
2. Wingspan (of that surface) in mm  
3. Fraction of the chord where center of lift is (leave this as 0.25, see what Romain said about C\_m)  
4. Forward left corner x coordinate  
5. Forward left corner y coordinate  
6. Either “wing” or “stabilizer”. Using “stabilizer” will simulate the airfoil being upside-down and will have its angle of attack influenced by the “tail incidence” value during analysis  
7. File name of the csv file containing lift, drag, and moment coefficient data for the airfoil. This file can be downloaded from [airfoiltools.com](http://airfoiltools.com) , but the first lines of generic information need to be removed first. This file needs to be in the “airfoils” folder  
   1. For some reason, it’s very difficult to reach the page you need by navigating the website, so use this url as a base and change it to get different airfoils or reynolds numbers: [http://airfoiltools.com/polar/details?polar=xf-naca4412-il-50000](http://airfoiltools.com/polar/details?polar=xf-naca4412-il-50000)  
      http://airfoiltools.com/polar/details?polar=xf-\[airfoil name\]-\[reynolds number\]  
      Then click on “download as csv file”  
      ![][image4]  
      The lines in the csv file highlighted in green need to be deleted before the calculator can use it.  
      Note: the algorithm uses a safety factor of 1.5 relative to the lift coefficients given by the csv (but you can change that easily if you want on line 9\)

**mate** \- defines a mate that can be used to connect this part to a mate on another part. Parameters are the name, x, and y coordinates (in mm). All mates within a part should have a unique name. Mates in different parts can share the same name if you want.

All parts automatically have a mate called “origin” defined at (0,0)

### Rods (Special Case for Parts) {#rods-(special-case-for-parts)}

To simulate a carbon fiber rod / tube it is simpler to use the rod mode. This is done by writing “specialtype:rod” on the FIRST LINE after “NEW PART”. After doing this, the part follows rules for rods, so most of the properties described above for generic parts will not work. Instead the following properties can be used:

Name, color, mate identical to generic parts

**dx** \- the distance in the forwards / backwards direction between each end of the rod  
**dy** \- the distance in the right/left direction between each end of the rod  
Lengthdensity \- linear density of the rod in g/mm

Note for rods: the coordinate system is pre-defined to have one end being the origin. Cg is automatically set to be at the center of the rod. Mates called “farend” and “center” are automatically added to the end of the rod that is not at the origin and middle of the rod.

### Assemblies {#assemblies}

The assembly is found before the first instance of “NEW PART” in the .madm file. The following functions can be used inside of the assembly section to build the model of the whole drone.

**add** \- adds a new part to the assembly. The first parameter is the name of the part that was defined in the part section. The second parameter is the new name you want to give the part in the assembled model. All parts in the model (2nd parameter) must have distinct names. See the lines that add the motors in the subscale

**attach** \- defines where in the model a part is to be connected so that a global coordinate system can be created. Syntax is “attach:partname1.matename1,partname2.matename2”

**modify** \- allows you to modify one of the properties of a part in the assemblies (useful if many similar parts but with one slight difference, and you don’t want to re-write the same thing a bunch of times in the parts section). So far this only works with **mass**, **rollcontrol** and **pitchcontrol**, since that’s all I needed it for, but I could make it work for other parts later if needed. 1st parameter is the name of the part to be modified, 2nd parameter is the name of the property to be overwritten, 3rd parameter is the new value

**pitchControl** \- a property of parts for use with motors which can only be added using modify in the assembly section. Defines how the flight-controller modifies thrust to induce a pitching moment. 0 means not used, \+1 means increase thrust to pitch up, \-1 means increase thrust to pitch down. If different motors have different gains, an intermediate value (like 0.7) can be used, but keep all of them between \-1 and 1\.

**rollControl** \- same as pitchControl property, but for roll. \+1 means increase thrust to roll right, \-1 means increase thrust to roll left.

## MADP Files {#madp-files}

These files define what analysis you want to perform on the drone model. I already created 2 that you can use for generic hover and horizontal flight stability. But you can modify these files or create a new one to calculate something different.

Every line in the file is executed sequentially (I got a bit carried away and basically invented a cheap scripting language). The following is a list of instructions you can use in the file, where the parameter is added after a “:” :

**vmax** \- maximum airspeed to use as the limit for aerodynamic graphs in m/s

**tailincidence** \- tail incidence angle (in degrees) to use during analysis. Multiple values can be added separated by “,”

**sethover** \- parameters (split by “,”) are vertical acceleration in m/s, pitching moment in Nm (positive is pitch up), and rolling moment in Nm (positive is roll right)

**printmotors** \- no parameters, outputs the thrust from each motors. Ideally use immediately after the sethover instruction

**graph:x\_moment** \- makes a graph of pitching moment against airspeed

**graph:AoA** \- makes a graph of angle of attack against airspeed

**graph:drag** \- makes a graph of drag against airspeed. Only takes into account wings and stabilizers under unrealistically ideal conditions. Ignores fuselage and wingtip vortices … True drag will be much higher

**graph:hover\_moments** \- makes a graph showing the possible moments that can be reached during hover at different thrust values. The vertical line shows the thrust required to reach equilibrium with the drone’s weight. This takes 2 additional parameters, separated by “,” the first indicates the control in the opposite axis, the second is either “C” or “M”.

- In “C” mode, the opposite control parameter is interpreted as being a raw output from  the flight controller (between \-1 and \+1). Setting this parameter to 0 means that all motors along the axis controlling the perpendicular axis have identical thrust, this does not necessarily indicate a moment of 0\.  
- In “M” mode, the opposite control parameter is interpreted as being the moment in the opposite axis.

**graph:hover\_moments3d** \- makes a 3D graph of hover stability. Axes are thrust, pitch moment, and roll moment. Does not have the same problems as the 2D slices, but is difficult to read from.

**modify** \- exactly the same as in .madm files

**label** \- overrides the default label (tail incidence \= \_)

**modelname** \- overrides the name of the model (appears on the title of each graph, default is the filename of the .madm file)

**newgraph**, **graphcombined**, and **showgraph** \- “graphcombined” can be used instead of “graph” to combine multiple graphs onto one (useful when using modify to change some aspect of the design and want to compare something. A combined graph must be preceded by newgraph, and end with showgraph (see “horizontal stability varying battery mass.madp” for an example)

## Usage {#usage}

![][image5]  
Run the python script (MAD Calc.py). A popup will ask you to select a .madm file, pick the one with the model for the drone you want to analyze. The total weight in grams should be printed, and a diagram of the drone should appear, double check it to make sure everything loaded properly and that the .madm file didn’t have any mistakes.

- Red circles indicate motors  
- Green areas represent wing surfaces  
- Orange areas represent stabilizer surfaces  
- Green and orange circles represent the center of lift of a wing or stabilizer surface  
- The circle with yellow and black rings shows the center of gravity of the whole drone  
- Other circles represent the center of gravity of individual parts (color depends on color parameter when defining the part in the .madm file, default is black)

![][image6]

If everything looks right, then enter “2” into the popup, then select the .madp file corresponding to the analysis you want to perform. **Expect to wait up to 30 seconds for some of the graphs to appear**. (I was too lazy to optimize my algorithms properly)  
![][image7]

Then you can enter “1” to select another drone model if you want to compare results between different designs, or “2” if you want to load another .madp and perform further analysis.

Then have fun reading all the graphs\!  
![][image8]
